topics.title: Spotting writers’ techniques
topics.intro: Writers choose techniques to create effects. In Year 7 you will name the technique AND explain its effect on the reader.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a simile and a metaphor.
topics.talk: Ask her to spot a simile or metaphor in a song lyric or advert.

topics.title: Punctuation for effect
topics.intro: Greater-depth writers use semi-colons, colons, dashes and brackets precisely. Let’s check what you already know.
topics.teach: Explain when to use a colon and when to use a semi-colon.
topics.talk: Ask her to find a semi-colon in a book and explain why it is there.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “The classroom was a zoo.”
items.explain: It says the classroom IS a zoo rather than LIKE one, so it is a metaphor.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “Her smile was as bright as the sun.”
items.explain: It compares using “as … as”, so it is a simile.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “The wind howled angrily through the trees.”
items.explain: Wind can’t really be angry or howl like a creature; giving it human feelings is personification.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “Seven slippery snakes slid silently.”
items.explain: Several nearby words start with the same sound (s).

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “Splash! Crash! Bang!”
items.explain: The words sound like the noises they describe.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “Do we really want our parks covered in litter?”
items.explain: It is asked for effect, not to get an answer.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “It was cold, dark and silent.”
items.explain: Three adjectives in a row make a memorable pattern.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “I’ve told you a million times!”
items.explain: It is a huge exaggeration for effect.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “Innocent puppies are being abandoned every single day.”
items.explain: Words like “innocent” and “abandoned” are chosen to make the reader feel sad or angry.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “The leaves danced in the breeze.”
items.explain: Leaves can’t dance; it gives them a human action.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “The fog was a grey blanket over the town.”
items.explain: It says the fog IS a blanket, so it is a metaphor.

items.prompt: Which technique is used here? “He ran like a cheetah.”
items.explain: It compares using “like”, so it is a simile.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a semi-colon correctly?

options.text: The rain fell; the river burst its banks.
The rain fell all night; the river.
options.feedback: A semi-colon must join two complete clauses. “The river” is not a complete clause.

options.text: I bought three kinds of fruit; apples and pears.
options.feedback: To introduce a list, use a colon, not a semi-colon.

options.text: Because it rained all night; we stayed in.
options.feedback: “Because it rained all night” cannot stand alone, so a semi-colon cannot follow it. Use a comma.

items.explain: A semi-colon joins two closely linked main clauses that could each be a sentence.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a colon correctly?

options.text: You will need: a torch, a map and a coat.
options.feedback: The part before a colon should be a complete clause. “You will need” is not complete on its own.

options.text: You need three things: a torch, a map and a coat.
I like: swimming, cycling and running.
options.feedback: A colon after “I like” breaks the sentence; no punctuation is needed there.

options.text: The old dog: barked loudly at the postman.
options.feedback: A colon cannot split the subject from its verb.

items.explain: A colon comes after a complete clause and introduces a list, an example or an explanation.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses brackets for parenthesis correctly?

options.text: My uncle (who lives in Wales) keeps bees.
My uncle who (lives in Wales) keeps bees.
options.feedback: The brackets must go round the whole extra information, including “who”.

options.text: (My uncle) who lives in Wales keeps bees.
options.feedback: The main sentence must still make sense without the bracketed part.

options.text: My uncle who lives (in Wales keeps bees).
options.feedback: Taking out the brackets here would leave “My uncle who lives”, which does not make sense.

items.explain: Parenthesis adds extra information. The sentence must still make sense if you remove it.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses dashes for parenthesis correctly?

options.text: The castle – built over 800 years ago – still stands.
The castle built – over 800 years ago still stands.
options.feedback: Dashes for parenthesis come in a pair, round the extra information.

options.text: The – castle built over 800 years ago – still stands.
options.feedback: Removing the dashed part leaves “The still stands”, which makes no sense.

options.text: The castle built over 800 years – ago still stands.
options.feedback: A single dash in the middle of a phrase breaks it.

items.explain: A pair of dashes works like brackets: the sentence makes sense without the part between them.

items.prompt: Which sentence is in the passive voice?

options.text: The window was smashed by a football.

options.feedback: Here the thing doing the action (the football) comes first. That is the active voice.
This is active, and it is not about the window at all.
This is a command (imperative), not passive.

items.explain: In the passive voice the thing that the action happens to comes first: “The window was smashed (by …)”.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses the subjunctive form?

options.text: If I were you, I would apologise.
If I was you, I would apologise.
options.feedback: In formal writing, use “were” after “If I …” for something imagined. This is the subjunctive.
This sentence does not make sense and has no subjunctive.

options.text: When I am you, I apologise.
options.feedback: This is not the subjunctive.

items.explain: The subjunctive is used in formal writing for wishes or imagined situations: “If I were…”, “I insist that he be…”.

items.prompt: Which sentence is the most formal?

options.text: We regret to inform you that the event has been cancelled.
Sorry, the event’s off, so don’t bother coming!
options.feedback: Contractions (“event’s”) and exclamations are informal.

options.text: The event is totally not happening, sorry.
options.feedback: “Totally” and “sorry” are chatty and informal.

options.text: Guess what? There’s no event after all, folks.
options.feedback: Questions like “Guess what?”, contractions and “folks” are very casual.

items.explain: Formal writing avoids contractions and chatty words, and often uses the passive voice.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a hyphen to avoid ambiguity?

options.text: I saw a man eating shark.
options.feedback: Without a hyphen this could mean a man was eating shark!

options.text: I saw a man – eating shark.
options.feedback: A dash is not a hyphen and changes the meaning.
The hyphen must join “man” and “eating”.

items.explain: A hyphen joins words to show they work together as one description: “man-eating”.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a relative clause?

options.text: The boy who won the race was beaming.
The boy won the race and was beaming.
options.feedback: This joins two clauses with “and”. A relative clause starts with who, which, that, whose, where or when.
This has an adjective, not a relative clause.

options.text: Winning the race, the boy beamed.
options.feedback: This starts with a fronted non-finite clause, not a relative clause.

items.explain: A relative clause adds information about a noun and starts with a relative pronoun such as who, which, that or whose.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a modal verb to show possibility?

options.feedback: This states a fact in the past; there is no modal verb.
This is the present progressive, not a modal verb.
This states a general fact.

items.explain: Modal verbs (might, could, should, will, must, may, can, would) show how likely or necessary something is.

sentences.title: Add a relative clause
sentences.prompt: Combine into ONE sentence using “who”: My grandma lives in Cornwall. My grandma makes amazing pasties.

checks.msg: Use “who” to join the sentences.
Keep the information about the pasties.
Keep the information about Cornwall.

sentences.model: My grandma, who lives in Cornwall, makes amazing pasties.
sentences.tip: Put the extra information straight after the noun it describes, between commas.

sentences.title: Relative clause with “which”
sentences.prompt: Combine into ONE sentence using “which”: The volcano erupted in 1980. The volcano is in the USA.

checks.msg: Use “which” to join the sentences.
Keep the date.
Keep where the volcano is.

sentences.model: The volcano, which is in the USA, erupted in 1980.
sentences.tip: Use “which” for things and “who” for people.

sentences.title: Join with a semi-colon
sentences.prompt: Join these two sentences with a semi-colon: The bell rang. Everyone rushed outside.

checks.msg: Put a semi-colon (;) between the two clauses, followed by a space.
After a semi-colon, carry on with a lower-case letter: “; everyone…”.

sentences.model: The bell rang; everyone rushed outside.
sentences.tip: A semi-colon joins two closely linked complete clauses. No capital letter after it.

sentences.title: Colon to introduce a list
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence that uses a colon to introduce a list of three things you would pack for a camping trip.

checks.msg: Use a colon (:) after a complete clause, then the list.
Separate list items with commas and put “and” before the last one.

sentences.model: I would pack three things: a tent, a torch and a sleeping bag.
sentences.tip: The part before the colon should make sense on its own.

sentences.title: Fronted adverbial
sentences.prompt: Rewrite so it starts with the adverbial and uses a comma: The fox crept across the garden as the sun went down.

checks.msg: Start with “As the sun went down,” followed by a comma.
Keep the rest of the sentence.

sentences.model: As the sun went down, the fox crept across the garden.
sentences.tip: When the adverbial comes first, put a comma after it.

sentences.title: Active to passive
sentences.prompt: Rewrite in the passive voice: The dog chewed the slipper.

checks.msg: Start with the thing the action happened to: “The slipper was chewed…”.
Add who did it: “by the dog”.

sentences.model: The slipper was chewed by the dog.
sentences.tip: Passive: thing affected + was/were + past participle (+ by whoever did it).

sentences.title: Parenthesis with brackets
sentences.prompt: Add extra information in brackets to this sentence: The Thames flows through London. (Extra info: the longest river entirely in England)

checks.msg: Put the extra information inside brackets ( ).
Include the extra information about it being the longest river.
Put the brackets straight after “The Thames”.

sentences.model: The Thames (the longest river entirely in England) flows through London.
sentences.tip: Read it without the brackets: it should still make sense.

sentences.title: Parenthesis with dashes
sentences.prompt: Add “a fearless explorer” as parenthesis using a pair of dashes: Ernest Shackleton led an expedition to Antarctica.

checks.msg: Put “– a fearless explorer –” between “Shackleton” and “led”, with a dash on each side.

sentences.model: Ernest Shackleton – a fearless explorer – led an expedition to Antarctica.
sentences.tip: Dashes for parenthesis always come in a pair.

sentences.title: Make it formal
sentences.prompt: Rewrite formally, with no contractions or chatty words: Hey, we can’t come to the meeting, sorry!

checks.msg: Remove informal words and contractions (hey, sorry, can’t).
Use formal words such as “unable”, “regret” or “unfortunately”.
Keep what you are writing about: the meeting.

sentences.model: Unfortunately, we are unable to attend the meeting.
sentences.tip: Formal: full forms (cannot), polite phrases, no exclamation marks.

sentences.title: Modal verbs for possibility
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence predicting what might happen in a story, using a modal verb (might, could, may, would or should).

checks.msg: Include a modal verb such as might, could or may.

sentences.model: The mysterious key might open the locked door in the cellar.
sentences.tip: Modal verbs show how certain you are.

sentences.title: Subordinate clause with “although”
sentences.prompt: Combine into ONE sentence starting with “Although”: It was raining. We went for a walk.

checks.msg: Start with “Although”.
Put a comma after the “although” clause.
Keep the walk.

sentences.model: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
sentences.tip: When a subordinate clause comes first, add a comma after it.

sentences.title: Expanded noun phrase
sentences.prompt: Expand “the house” into a noun phrase of at least five words with two adjectives and a prepositional phrase, then use it in a sentence.

checks.msg: Add a prepositional phrase (e.g. “on the hill”).
Keep “house” in your noun phrase.
Put adjectives before “house”.

sentences.model: The crumbling, silent house on the hill watched us.

sentences.title: Cohesive adverbial
sentences.prompt: Write a second sentence that begins with a cohesive adverbial (e.g. However, As a result, Meanwhile, Furthermore). First sentence: The bridge was closed for repairs.

checks.pattern: ^(However|As a result|Meanwhile|Furthermore|Consequently|Therefore|Nevertheless|In addition|On the other hand|Because of this),
checks.msg: Start with an adverbial such as “As a result,” followed by a comma.

sentences.model: As a result, drivers had to take a long detour.
sentences.tip: Cohesive adverbials link ideas between sentences and paragraphs.

sentences.title: Show, don’t tell
sentences.prompt: Instead of writing “Sam was scared”, write a sentence that SHOWS Sam was scared through actions or body language. Don’t use “scared”, “afraid” or “frightened”.

checks.msg: Don’t name the feeling. Show it through what Sam does.
Write about Sam.

sentences.model: Sam’s hands trembled as he edged towards the creaking door.
sentences.tip: Think about hands, breathing, voice, eyes and movement.

sentences.title: Analytical sentence
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence explaining the effect of this phrase: “the icy fingers of the wind”. Use the word “suggests” or “conveys”.

checks.msg: Use an analysis verb such as “suggests” or “conveys”.
Refer to the words or the technique used.

sentences.model: The personification of “icy fingers” suggests the wind is grasping and cruel, as if it wants to hurt people.
sentences.tip: Name the technique, quote the words, then explain the effect on the reader.

sentences.title: Punctuate direct speech
sentences.prompt: Write this as direct speech with correct punctuation: Mia asked where the treasure was hidden.

checks.msg: Put Mia’s exact words in speech marks, starting with a capital and ending with a question mark inside the speech marks.
Say who is speaking (Mia asked…).

sentences.model: “Where is the treasure hidden?” asked Mia.
sentences.tip: The question mark goes inside the speech marks.
